passage: The power had gone out at the roadside tea stall, and rain hammered the tin roof. Jomon, the cook, sliced through a cloth-wrapped onion in the dark and cut his hand. Blood ran between his fingers onto the wet floor. Rafiq, who had done the college first-aid course in spring, felt his heart race. He made himself check first: the knife was set aside, the floor was slippery, nobody else was near. "Someone call 112," he said, and named a customer. He took a clean cloth and pressed firmly on the cut, holding it there. "Sit down, Jomon, I've got you." He did not lift the cloth to look until help arrived.

passage: In the housing society compound, a boy of nine skidded off his cycle and gashed his knee on the gravel. Sarita, his mother, ran out with her hand over her mouth. Lavanya was passing with her groceries. She had finished a first-aid course last year and her hands were steady, though her chest was tight. First she checked the road was clear and moved the cycle aside. "Sarita, call 112 and give the gate number." Then she pressed a clean cloth on the knee and kept the boy sitting. She spoke calmly, "I am here, it will be all right." When the ambulance came, she told them only what she had done.

passage: In the college hostel common room, Joseph cut his palm on a broken glass while washing up. Blood ran down his wrist. People shouted. Alka, twenty, who had done a first-aid course last term, felt her heart jump, then her training kicked in. She checked for more glass on the floor, moved people back and said, "Someone call the warden and the ambulance, now." She took a clean towel, pressed it firmly on the cut and asked Joseph to hold his hand up. She didn't try to pull anything out of the wound or clean it; that wasn't what she'd been taught to do. She kept talking to him calmly until the warden arrived with the nurse.

passage:
Dear Karthik,

You asked if the first-aid course was worth it. Let me tell you what happened on Saturday.

At the bus stand, a woman tripped on the kerb and cut her forehead. There was a lot of blood and people just stared. I was scared, honestly. But I remembered the steps. I checked that no bus was coming. I asked a shopkeeper to call 108. I pressed my clean handkerchief on the cut and asked her to sit down. That's all. I didn't try to do more than we'd been taught.

The ambulance came in fifteen minutes. The paramedic said the pressure helped.

So yes, do the course.

Yamini

qa.a: Yamini felt scared, but the practised steps brought steadiness.

qa.a: Yamini checked for traffic, got someone to call 108 and pressed a clean handkerchief on the cut, without attempting more than the course taught.

qa.q: How might Karthik be affected by the letter?
qa.a: Karthik might feel encouraged to do the course, seeing how simple steps made a real difference.

grounding: A letter describes a trained young adult checking for danger, calling for help and applying pressure, while knowing the limits of the training.

subtype: Basic first aid course and calm hands [Actor]
passage: You asked why I made everyone at the cricket club do first aid. I'm Uday. Last summer, during a practice match, my teammate Mehak was hit on the eyebrow by a ball. There was blood everywhere, and the others were shouting and angry at the bowler. I'd done a first-aid course. I remember feeling angry too, then forcing myself to breathe. First, I stopped the match so no more balls would come. I told the coach to call an ambulance. I pressed a clean towel on the cut and made Mehak sit still. I didn't try to check the eye or give any medicine; that's for doctors. The paramedics took over. That's all first aid is: danger, call, pressure, wait.

qa.a: Knowing the limits of first aid is part of the skill; those tasks are for doctors.

qa.a: Mehak was probably frightened and in pain, but steadier with someone calm taking charge.

Saturday: At the college first-aid workshop, the instructor made Ritu repeat it until it bored her: "Danger. Call. Press. And don't do anything you weren't taught."
Two weeks later, Thursday: A glass slipped from Karthik's hand in the hostel kitchen and a long shard sliced his palm. Blood dripped fast onto the floor, and he swore at himself, furious. Ritu's stomach flipped, but the words came in order. She kicked the broken pieces away from their feet. "Mehul, call the warden and ask for the doctor, now." She folded a clean tea towel, pressed it hard on the cut and held his hand up. A tiny sliver glinted near the edge. She wanted to pick it out. She didn't.
Friday: Karthik came back with stitches and a bandage. "The doctor took out a piece of glass," he said. "Said the pressure helped." Ritu nodded. "I nearly tried to take it out myself."

qa.a: A folded clean tea towel.

qa.a: Her stomach flipped with fear, but she stayed calm enough for the practised words to come in order.

qa.a: She wanted to pick out the glass sliver but didn't, leaving it for the doctor and sticking to pressure, which she had been taught.

qa.q: How might Karthik see the moment afterwards?
qa.a: Karthik was angry at himself during it, and afterwards is probably grateful, since the doctor said the pressure helped.
